I was hoping that they would hear me and come out and see why was somebody crying out in pain so much, why were they killing -- beating up people without any reason whatsoever? So Predojevic at a certain point, after they had had their fill of beating me up, said, "Get the cattle out of here. Let him die out there." So they took me out and I went and joined the other camp inmates on the pista. I was dying of thirst. I was asking for water. Fortunately there was a bottle of water. Nikola Matanovic, who was a Croat, he luckily had some water; he was also a haulier, and he gave me that water and I drank it up. They tried to do something with me, they put some dressings on my wounds, and they covered my bruises with them, some makeshift dressings. Anyway, I managed to survive and here I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the names of the guards Predojevic, Paspalj. Did you recognise any other persons who beat you? Were these the same persons that you mentioned earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Paspalj and Predojevic are the same Paspalj and Predojevic. I don't know the other ones. I would recognise them if I saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sustain any injuries due to this beating?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: My thoracic bone, my thorax, the right-side of my chest, was broken. My legs were also very weak. I tried to do some bowling, I can't do it any more. I used to play football before, I can't do that any more either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other instances that you were beating during the time that you were detained in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: We would be beaten up as we went to lunch or as we went out to use the lavatory. I talked to the other inmates. This was something quite ordinary. This was not counted as -- considered some special beating. What was considered a special beating was when you were individually singled out and taken out to be beaten. But this was something quite normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody, any people who were in authority intervene when this kind of beating happened? Especially the time that you were beaten, did they intervene to stop that or prevent it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware as to whether any of these guards who were involved in this kind of abuse or misconduct were ever punished?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No. To my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were taken to the first floor of a building. Which building was that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: That was the administration building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that they tried to help you with the dressing. Who are these people whom you referred to as "they," after you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: The inmates who were on the pista.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other detainees.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes. The very fact that they just gave me some water helped immensely immediately after that beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long were you detained in Omarska, the total extent of time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I left Omarska on the 28th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you describe to the Court how you were transferred to the other place and what took place during your transfer.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: There were cases of lads, 17 years of age, who had muscular dystrophy and who couldn't go out by themselves, and then there were other elderly and invalid people. So Esad asked that these people should be released. There were other detainees who reported to the doctor with different ailments and pains, so that Dr. Ivic one day arrived in Omarska. I knew him from before and I told him, "Please get me out of here because they're going to kill me." They returned me to Mujo's room again, and after some 15 minutes they called my name and we went out onto the pista to go home. There were 100 of us chosen to go home, mostly elderly people. That night we did not go home because there was not fuel for that. Then we were transferred to the hangar, upstairs to the offices, in fact, that were there. There we spent another three days, and then that day came, when in the morning Marmat was roll-calling the people, and said, "When I call out your names, you will have to state your address and your name and your number." So we left the hangar and went downstairs. The bus was parked downstairs, and when we -- we had another roll-call by Marmat in front of the bus as well. As I was departing for home, before that Mladen Radic was present there during the roll-call. Marmat called again the people's names, and when he said Zlatan Blazevic, he said,"You are the one. You go back." Zlatan went back. We boarded the bus and went to Trnopolje. We actually thought we were going home, but we went westward and were driven to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the second time that you were called out, a person by the name of Marmat called you out.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was this person?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: He was a mechanic for bulldozers, and he worked in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he in the camp, in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: There he was a guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he dressed? Was he armed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was armed. He wore a blue summer uniform, a policeman's blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there was this person who you referred to as Krkan was present. Is this the same person whom you testified earlier as Krkan?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he dressed? Did you see him then?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was also wearing a blue policeman's uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he armed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he doing there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: He was standing there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a person by the name of Zlatan Blazevic who was stopped heading into the bus?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Blazevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who stopped him getting into the bus?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: It was Marmat who said, "You are the one. You go back." As far as I could see, as far as I could sense, when we were being roll-called to board the bus, I think it was Marmat. But I did hear someone say, "You are the one. You go back."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person Marmat, did you see him often in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know as to which shift or what time he worked, in whose shift he worked?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: He worked in Mladjo's shift. It was a 12-hour shift, from 7.00 a.m. to 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you name this shift in the name of these people, such as Krkan?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Because that's how they were called. All the detainees said, for instance, "Tomorrow we have Krkan's shift," and there was another guard, commander, whose name was Ckalja. Of course, that was a nickname. We would also refer to his shift as Ckalja's shift. Then there was a third one named Krle, and that was his shift, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting but I see that Mr. Fila wanted to intervene perhaps with regard to Mladja. He is Mladjo, I believe; is that right? Go ahead, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says Mahmut as well in the transcript where it should be Marmat. Marmat. If he were Mahmut, he would be a Muslim. That's the first thing. Secondly, when the witness says Mladjo Radic, the Prosecutor should not refer to him as Krkan. When the witness says Krkan, then it's all right for him to say Krkan, but they should stick to the names given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We always have problems with names. But I know that the court reporters revise their work and correct it afterwards. But, yes, if the witness says Mladjo Radic, then indeed that name should be repeated and not be referred to as Krkan. Please go ahead, Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I will. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person whom you referred to as -- sorry. Witness, the person whom you referred to as Marmat, could you explain as to whether he was referred to as Marmat?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes, Marmat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen Zlatan Blazevic thereafter in the camp, thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in Trnopolje --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were transferred to Trnopolje. How were you transferred?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: By bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were in the bus, and who were they?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: There were civilians. There were Muslims and Croats there as well. 99 of us were transported in two buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were the detainees who were with you in Omarska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Trnopolje before you were released?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I stayed in Trnopolje for two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you come out of that place?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: That day, when I left Trnopolje, I went to the medical centre. There were a lot of people who were ill. And I went to see a doctor to ask him to give me some pills, and I met Zoran Tomicevic, a Serb soldier, at the infirmary. I knew him, we worked together. He found it difficult to recognise me because I had lost 36 kilograms. I said hello to him and I greeted him too, and he said, "Would you like to go home?" And I thought he was joking, and he said, "Yes, really. If you want to I'll take you home." And then he went to ask permission. He asked Slobodan Kuruzovic whether I could go home, and he said that that can't be done that way, that there was certain procedure. But Zoran just took a list and wrote my name and surname on the list, where it had been said that I had been killed, and then he told me to get into the car. We got into his blue Golf, and he took me to my own backyard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went home to your house in Raskovac.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: From Trnopolje we stopped off in a cafe called Grmec which existed before the war. We went there and then from that cafe we went to my house. He brought me to my own yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At home, were the other members of your family present?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get to know what happened to them in your absence?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I learnt that they had been in Trnopolje, my two sons and my wife, and they left Trnopolje, they came home, and I found them at home when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your testimony you referred to a person by the name of Mladjo Radic, also known as Krkan.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look around the courtroom and indicate as to whether you can identify or cannot that person.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: That's Mladen Radic, sitting there in the back row, to the left. When I look at him, he is to the left. Otherwise, he is to the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you say how he is dressed?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: He's wearing a suit with a tie and a red shirt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell from the door his position from the security officer who is seated there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: He is next to the guard, the first from the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: It may be noted, Your Honour, that the witness identifies the accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also referred to -- testified about a person by the name of Miroslav Kvocka, whom you said that you knew earlier. Could you look around the court and identify, or could you see and identify whether he is present in court today.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes. Miroslav Kvocka is sitting next to Radic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: It may be noted that the witness identifies the accused. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said that you went home and you stayed in your house. Until when -- did you leave Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of November, it was a Wednesday, of 1992, I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the time that you came home and the time that you left Bosnia, where were you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, my question was: From the time you came from Trnopolje and the time that you left the country, were you at home?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to -- what was the condition? Were you able to move around freely?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't even allowed to cough. My wife was so frightened, and if I would cough at night she would put my hand over my mouth so that the sound couldn't be heard, because she didn't want them to know that there was a male in the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For you to leave Bosnia, did you have to do anything in order to leave?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I had to sign papers that I was handing over my house, my car, and my little summer house, that I was bequeathing everything that I had. I just took a bag with photographs, my family photographs, with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the family go with you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you explain to the Court what long-term effects, if any, whether psychological or physical, setbacks that you have had due to the detention in the camp and the conditions that you faced in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I have physical repercussions. My ribs were broken. Psychological as well. I get up in the middle of the night and have to smoke and walk around; this isn't too frequent but it does happen, especially if I look at the television and see Omarska on it. Of course, when you see pictures, this reminds you of all your own images, people who were beaten up and mistreated in the camp, the times when we went to lunch -- it wasn't actually lunch, the food was so bad, but anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said that when you left Bosnia that you had to hand over and sign papers giving your property. To whom were these papers signed and given?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Well, the people who were patrolling. They were wearing the uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army and you knew that they were Serbs because of their uniform. And they patrolled my street and they said that we were not allowed to take anything out of the house, and if they saw us, this wouldn't be a good thing. So they said that we were not to take anything. And we went into the shed. And all the people who were to leave Prijedor had to sign away their property, sign pieces of paper granting them a permit to leave town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to leave your country, did you have to pay any money to any organisation?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I, for example, paid -- that is to say, I had to send in all the bills. I didn't have any heating, but I had to pay heating bills. I had to pay for the sort of central heating which I didn't have, and other papers that I had to sign and other bills. And when I got all these papers, I went to the Red Cross and they issued a sort of permit allowing us to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: That will be the end of the direct examination of this witness, Your Honour. I seek your permission to make a correction with regard to the exhibits which I would intend to produce at the end of the cross-examination -- re-examination. The exhibit item number which was referred to as 3/77A originally, and marked and produced, as the witness marked certain -- made some markings, I would mark it afresh as it would be a new exhibit, and mark it as 3/92. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Waidyaratne. Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have not had occasion to make any agreements, so we will follow the order of the indictment, and if any of the Defence counsel have questions, they will cross-examine the witness in that order, which means that I will be the first to begin with the cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is the order in which the accused are listed in the indictment. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are now going to answer questions which are going to be put to you by Defence counsel. The first will be Mr. Krstan Simic who has some questions for you. You have the floor, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. K. Simic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alisic, you have already heard that I am Defence counsel for Mr. Kvocka, and I have several questions for you linked to your examination-in-chief today. You said that you know Prijedor well because you lived there ever since birth.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like us to try and clarify a little bit, for everyone's benefit, the path, the route, from the car market to the SUP building where you stopped for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us where the car market is in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: It is in my street, Muharema Seljanovica Street, next to the leather factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it a densely populated part of town?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is the SUP building from the car market, or rather could you describe the path the bus took?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I could. The bus I was in passed by the market, turned right towards the SDK building, the bank, then turned left next to the town planning building, past the stadium; then you turn right and you come to where Safet's cafe used to be, called Rudar; then you turn right, next to the old Balkan Hotel, and then straight ahead to the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long is that whole route? You're a driver so you know it well.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: With all the turnings, it is about 1.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I know Prijedor well too, let us confirm once again, are these roads, town roads, roads with buildings on both sides, housing estates?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: There are no private houses there; there are just apartment buildings. If you know Prijedor well, the stadium is there so there are no houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony, you mentioned that you were sitting on the right-hand side, next to the window, in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't mention which row of seats.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I was roughly in the middle of the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So about the tenth row?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: About the middle of the bus, or to be more precise, I was right next to the door in the middle of the bus, because this was a bus with three doors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the route from the car market to the SUP building, where you stopped for the first time, you spoke of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see those bodies, in which streets?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I said that I saw them when we reached the market, the green market. There's a kiosk on the right-hand side there. In front of that kiosk, I saw some bodies. On the left-hand side, on the pavement, I saw bodies. Actually, that is where my street intersects with the street of the market.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alisic, are we talking about corpses seen from the bus or once you reached the market?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: From the bus. As we reached the market, there were bodies at the market and I saw them from the bus. The bus was mobile; it was moving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: On both the left and the right-hand side. On the right there's a kiosk; I saw some dead civilians there, to my right, as we were going, to my right, on my right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You frequently stressed the fact that you saw people wearing uniforms of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other kinds of uniforms in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, at the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Not in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were the only uniforms that existed there.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I also served the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now try and clarify the circumstances linked to your arrival in Omarska. Could you tell us more closely what time it could have been?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: It was dark, I know. I know that it was 2.30 when I left my house; I know that for sure. First the women and children were boarded onto buses, and the elderly; then they started boarding us. Whether I was in the first or the third or the fifth bus, I really don't know. It's very difficult to tell. But it was just before darkness fell that we reached Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alisic, in your testimony you mentioned that at the time when arriving at Omarska, you noticed three persons whom you named as Predojevic, Popovic, and Paspalj; you said that you knew those persons very well from before, and you described your contacts with them, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us the first names of those people? Because you only used their surnames.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not one of their first names?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to the moment when you actually arrived in Omarska. You said that there was a bus in front of you and then your bus. Were there other buses behind you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far was your bus from the bus in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: They were one next to the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. You knew Mr. Predojevic well.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I have described how I met him. We met in the timber yard and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but we're talking about his identification. So there is no doubt that the person who shot at that time was Mr. Predojevic, whom you knew and whom you have described.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, since you said there were six persons, were all six killed or were any wounded?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: They were all dead. They were lying on the asphalt. No one moved, not one of them moved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the shooting, and when those six persons lay on the asphalt, as you say, dead, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: The order was for the next six men to come out with their hands behind their heads, and then they would say that we had to go on towards the entrance of the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was the procedure for each group of six.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes. We would go one by one, hands against the walls, searching. Name, surname, year of birth, address, we had to give those particulars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Roughly how much time passed between the shooting and your entrance into the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Roughly 20 minutes or a half hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any vehicle or ambulance arrive?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear it coming later?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went straight to Mujo's room.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony you said that there were very many people, too many people there, and that you were put up in the toilet, together with some others.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you arrived at Mujo's room, were there other men coming to Mujo's room?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they put up?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: To the hall in front of the toilet, to Mujo's room. We were overcrowded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony you mentioned the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes, those who questioned us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they work?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: They worked on the upstairs floor of the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often during your stay there did you climb upstairs to the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Twice; when I was beaten and when I was interrogated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I was interrogated roughly in the second half of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not questioned on the 4th of June?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In front of the investigators' room, did you see any investigators there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were interrogated, in what room did that take place?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: The second room to the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the investigators?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: There was a moustached, shorter man from Banja Luka, Brka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to Trnopolje, you mentioned Zoran Tomasevic [sic].

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Tomicevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Tomicevic. Who is Zoran Tomicevic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: He is an auto mechanic like me. We went to school together and then he went to advance training. Then he was in a department called the hygienic technical safety department; HTZ, it was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of your education and occupation, would you say that he was an important person?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't, not really, though we were good friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slobodan Kuruzovic, what was he?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Kuruzovic was a teacher of mathematics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in Trnopolje. What was he there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Kuruzovic was the commander of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zoran Tomicevic, did he have any military rank?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I don't know. He didn't wear any insignia on his uniform. He wore a JNA camouflage uniform, but he didn't wear any insignia of rank on his shoulder or on his collar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A man of no great importance, without any rank, comes and writes down that you are killed, and you leave. During your testimony you said that there were extremists who would come and no one could do anything to them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony, you mentioned when you went to the hangar. Was there a wire fence?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: A wire fence? Yes. The points were at a distance of 15 centimetres; the distance between the spikes was 15 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there was an area encircled by barbed wire in the hangar. Could you tell us what it encircled, that barbed wire?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: That barbed wire was in front of us, to the side, where there is a big gate for large trucks of 110 tonnes. From that door to the end of the second wall was barbed wire, and it was about one metre, twenty high, the barbed wire fence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back to the event of the 30th of April. Did you personally see the shooting and the killing of six men?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anyone you knew, apart from these three persons that you mentioned, Predojevic, Paspalj, I think, and Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you manage to hear the words spoken by Predojevic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I heard them loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they uttered before, during, or after the shooting?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: After the shooting. After he opened fire, the men fell and then he said, "Balija, you should know where you have come and what lies in store for you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alisic, I have no further questions for you. Thank you very much for your answers. I deeply regret everything you have been through.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Krstan Simic. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Milojica Kos will not cross-examine Mr. Alisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Fila, it is your turn now. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I shall be very, very brief. Cross-examined by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alisic, after all your suffering I don't want to make you suffer any more, so I shall be very brief. You mentioned barbed wire. Were the trucks behind that fence? What was the purpose of that fence?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: There were no inmates there. We were the first group to go there. My group went there, and I found the barbed wire fence already there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was there to protect those trucks?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No. I've just explained. I've shown you from what gate to which wall, and we were in that area, within the barbed wire fence, right next to the main wall. And there was a passage through which we passed and that is where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How high was the fence?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: It was about one metre, one metre, twenty; about four or five rows of these wires.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you said that there were three shifts.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that they worked from 7.00 to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes, from 7.00 to 7.00, 12 hours each. A day shift and a night shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happens when a shift works from 7.00 in the morning until 7.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Then the next shift comes from 7.00 in the evening until 7.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Then the other one that was free during the day takes over, again from 7.00 in the morning to 7.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So one shift was always free. What happens after the third shift?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: The one that worked during the night would be free the next day, and then it would be on duty the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Very well. You said that when you arrived -- the first day was the 30th of May, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That you found those guards there and that those guards were in Krkan's shift; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did Krkan's shift come on duty again the next time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Krkan's shift should come -- if it was working the night shift, then it would be free the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was on duty when you arrived.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time that it was Mladjo Radic's shift. I didn't know who was a guard or where I had come to or anything, I knew nothing at all, or who were the shift leaders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to that. But when did you see Krkan for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I saw him maybe after I had stayed there for two days. Perhaps two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes, a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all I wanted to know. If you came in the evening, that was before 7.00, I assume, before darkness fell.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't be so specific. I really don't remember the hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. I know that. How could you? But if you say it was Krkan's shift, was it the night shift or was it the last hours of the day shift?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I think it must have been the night shift. I said that when I arrived in the camp -- I never allege that it was Krkan's shift. I just said that Popovic, Paspalj, and Predojevic were in Krkan's shift. That day when I arrived, I didn't mention Krkan's shift. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you mentioned these three names.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then later on you said that they were members of Krkan's shift.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Was that the night shift when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I think it was the night shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it was the night shift, then its turn would come again when?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: This was a Saturday, so they should have been free on Sunday and they should have come again on Monday, for the morning. That was the timetable of the shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was Saturday, until Sunday morning; then from Sunday morning until Monday morning, it couldn't have been the same shift.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were watching the changing of shifts. What did that look like?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: First of all, we didn't hear what people were saying. Two buses would come. The guards would go out who were on duty. If Mladjo Radic was the shift leader, he would line them up, speak to them. I wouldn't hear what he said. I saw them, though, because I was on the pista. The same applied to Ckalja or Kos; they would line them up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would a flag be raised?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anything sung?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You used to come to this facility before.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a water supply system there?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is the same water supply system that existed before and when you were there in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same water that flowed before flowed when you were there.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I assume so. The same taps were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same water, yes. You mentioned a person Cvitan and then Pavlic or Pavsic.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about that name, but all the inmates know him. They called him Cvitan, and the guards too, and the reason was he had a strand of white hair here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is whether that is one and the same person.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know which shift he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Because I know the composition. Popovic, Paspalj, Predojevic, he was there, and then someone called Marmat. We got to know that shift because it was Mladjo Radic's shift, because the beatings were the worst by Paspalj, Predojevic, and Popovic. It was unbearable, and it's normal that one should remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that to be so, as this has been repeated in other testimonies. Apart from these men, how many others were in that shift?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: You mean in the same shift?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Once when we were on the pista we wanted to count them, and we didn't manage because you dare not really look in one direction for too long. I think there were between 30 and 40 men in one shift. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from these names that you have enumerated, do you remember any other names from the same shift?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I know their faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not their names?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can I conclude that the judgement that you made of Krkan's shift was based on the behaviour of these four men?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you said that you never noticed him being present when this was happening.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever notice him giving orders? The Prosecutor asked you whether anyone protected you. But did you notice him giving orders to any one of these four?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can one infer from that, at least as an assumption, that they may have done this arbitrarily, of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: It could, but we, as inmates, felt that the shift leaders and the camp commanders should protect us, and we expected them to protect us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did the guards have to have special orders, or did they act of their own free will?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes. They didn't need any orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they acted arbitrarily?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding Cvitan and Pavlic, do you know what his surname is?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: The surname was Pavletic, I think. But Cvitan, everybody knows him by his nickname, Cvitan.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That would be all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. Mr. Tosic, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Zoran Zigic has no questions or cross-examination for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Jovan Simic. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] We have no questions either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Waidyaratne, any additional questions, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Just to clear up one matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Okay. Re-examined by Mr. Waidyaratne:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Learned counsel for the accused Radic, Mr. Fila, asked you with regard to two names. He referred you to the person by the name of Pavlic and another by the name of Cvitan. Were they the same person?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: That's all. Your Honour, I would tender the exhibit numbers which have been marked through this witness, 3/77 -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. It should be 3/90, 3/91, and 3/92; 3/90 is the photograph of the model of the Omarska camp; 3/91 is the photograph where the witness and the victim who was referred to as Gordan Kardumovic are seen; and 3/92 was the diagram where the witness marked certain places. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before ruling on this request, I wish to give the floor to Judge Wald for her questions. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Alisic, you testified, I believe, that there was a time when a truck came and dead bodies were loaded onto the truck, and you saw this from your position on the pista, and you also saw that Mr. Kvocka was nearby. Can you tell me approximately how many dead bodies were loaded onto that truck and whether or not you had seen those dead bodies there for any period before the truck came and took them away?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: It was a Sunday, and the truck came, that is true, and the bodies were loaded onto it. There were roughly ten bodies, ten or so bodies. I had not seen those people before. I saw them being loaded and driven off, and the driver's name was Vlado Kobas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is: You mentioned that, I believe, if I remember correctly, that you had known or at least had had an acquaintance with these few men, Paspalj and Predojevic, who had beaten you. I wondered whether or not at any point in the beatings did they give you any reason for why they were singling you out, at that time, for these especially brutal beatings, with the whips with the iron, or whatever it was, balls at the end? Was there any explanation, why you?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: In your experience, did you know, see, or hear about others getting this kind of beating with the whips with the irons at the end?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My last question is: You told us that you recognised some of the people as guards and that at least after you had been at Omarska a while you knew that Mr. Radic was a shift commander, and you mentioned seeing several times Mr. Kvocka whom you had some acquaintance with before Omarska. What role did you think Mr. Kvocka was playing? A guard, a shift commander, or something else in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Kvocka was, at first, the camp commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did you learn or understand that to be so from what you heard from other inmates, or was there some other source from which you knew that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: We learned that when we were taken to the pista. Miroslav Kvocka said that himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Witness, I personally have two questions. The first: You said that when Plavsic beat Nasic, Kvocka was next -- was right there. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You marked the position on Exhibit 3/92. Was Kvocka inside the restaurant or outside?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Outside the restaurant, next to Cvitan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Outside. Thank you. My second question: When you were beaten by Paspalj and Predojevic, you said that you expected Kvocka or Radic to come out to prevent this mistreatment. Why did you expect that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: I expected that because I knew that Radic was shift leader and Kvocka, the camp commander. They were superiors to the men who were beating me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that point in time did you know whether he was present in the camp or not?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: In that same corridor are the offices where they usually stayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that he was almost always there. If you don't know, never mind. Did you know, at that particular time when you were beaten, did you know whether he was present in the camp or not on that particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the circumstances, if he were present, would it be possible for him to hear your cries?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD ALISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. I should now like to turn to the Defence to hear from them whether they have any objections to the admission of the exhibits that the Prosecutor has tendered. Mr. Simic, are you speaking on behalf of all of your colleagues? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I'm speaking on behalf of the whole Defence team. We have no objections to the admission of the documents tendered by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. So the exhibits listed by Mr. Waidyaratne are admitted into evidence. Witness, you have finished -- Mr. Mirsad Alisic, you have finished your testimony before this Tribunal. You have answered a large number of questions put to you. Do you have anything you would like to declare that hasn't yet been said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to wish that nobody should go through what we went through again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness, very much, and we share with you those wishes. We would also hope that no one should suffer what you and others have suffered, and we wish you a happy journey home. Thank you very much. The usher will escort the witness out, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have 30 minutes more. I think we could proceed with the next witness. The Prosecution calls Witness Okic Jasmir, if it's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we should have a brief break because I think we have been working since 11.30, so it's been a long spell. I think we must have at least a ten-minute break, and then we'll resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May I, for the Prosecution, call Witness Okic Jasmir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're waiting for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going to read the solemn declaration handed to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. 22

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, please. Are you comfortable, Mr. Jasmir Okic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First you're going to answer questions which Mr. Waidyaratne is going to put to you. You have the floor, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Waidyaratne:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please state your name to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: Jasmir Okic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your date of birth and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 3rd of November, 1959, in Rahima Bajramovica Street, Raskovac, Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: I am a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: I have three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old are they?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: One was born in 1984, the second in 1987, and the third in 1997. The first two are girls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: Before the war I lived in Rahima Bajramovica Street, in the Raskovac neighbourhood of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you school, and what is your education and qualifications?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: I completed the primary school in Prijedor, the secondary school for locksmiths also in Prijedor, and the advance school for specialist locksmiths also in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perform compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When and where?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: I did my military service from August 1978 to November 1979 in Karlovac and in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you specialise in any -- or did you have any special courses, follow any special courses, during your service?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I underwent training for section leader in Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "section leader"?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: There was commander of a smallest group of soldiers, up to ten, a squad, and then a company comes later. But I was the leader of a group of ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your employment, your occupation in -- up to 1985?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: Until 1985? Until 1985 I worked as a locksmith in Bosna Montaza, Prijedor. We were working on steel structures, producing steel structures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After 1985, did you work in any other place?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: In 1985, I transferred to another company, Impro, it was called, the industry of meat products in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve in the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From when and where?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the reserve police force from May 1980 until April 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you serve?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: Until September 1991, throughout that period, we would have two or three exercises every year. We had lectures, shooting exercises. And from September 1991 until April 1992 I worked in the Prijedor police station, as part of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from September 1991, you were mobilised.

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why you were mobilised during that time?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: We were mobilised because of the security situation. The active-duty police were designated to the local communities where they lived, and we, the reserve force, were called up to report to the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by the "security situation"? Could you explain or describe to us what it is?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: The security situation was tense because of the war in Croatia, and this had certain repercussions in our area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the functions of the reserve policemen at the time when you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: When I was mobilised, I was on patrol and for a time I stood guard at the bridge across the Sana River, near the Prijedor Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you attached to, which police station?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: I was attached to the Prijedor centre police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you worked until April of 1992. Do you remember in the month of April which date it was that you stopped work or you last worked?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: My last working day, I was the third shift on the 28th of April, and I finished on the 29th, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go back to work thereafter, after the 29th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, the Serbs took over power in Prijedor, and when they did that, the men in the third shift, all the non-Serb policemen were disarmed and returned home. And the next shift that arrived, also the non-Serbs in that shift were disarmed and told to go home. And that is why I didn't go back to work either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you refer to non-Serbs. Do you know or did you come to know any persons, or could you name any persons who didn't report to work after the 29th?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: For instance, Mirsad Alisic, Tahir Cirkic, Cirkic Enver, Nedzad Besic, Crgic Hasan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you served as a reserve policeman, were you provided with a weapon and a uniform?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had a rifle and a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do with the weapon that you were provided with?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: I returned the weapon in the second half of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom did you return the weapon?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: My colleague who worked with me, Nedzad Besic called me up. He had returned his weapon, and he said it would be a good idea to contact the SUP. I contacted Radenko, he came to the local community, and that is where we handed in the weapons and uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, may I ask this question at this stage: Were you a member of any other military or paramilitary group?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take part in any of these attacks or uprisings in the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I will draw your attention to the 30th of May, 1992. Do you remember that date?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of May, I was at home. On the 30th of May, or rather a day or two before, I buried my father and I was tired, so that on the 30th of May I slept late. And then my cousin's wife arrived and said, "You're sleeping and there's shooting in town." So I got up, and with my family I moved over to my nephew's house, together with my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this nephew's house in Raskovac?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The house was next to mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you were there, in your nephew's house?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: While we were there, in the afternoon, a Serb soldier in an olive-green uniform came to the door and he said, "You can take what you have with you and come out and go towards the centre of town, because you're not coming back here again."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you adhere to these orders?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and I headed down the road. There were lots of other civilians and soldiers. At the end of the road, there was a tank with Serb soldiers on it who were showing the three-finger sign and yelling and shouting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear what they said and what they shouted at that time?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: They were shouting "Do Jaja."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean? Can you explain what it meant? Did you understand what it was?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: It meant going to the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that these Serb soldiers who were on top of the tank had the three-finger --

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: Yes, three fingers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: It meant one president, one state, one people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you proceed from your home?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: We went towards Prijedor, along the old road towards Skela, for a kilometre or a kilometre and a half. We reached a field next to the old leatherworks; that is where we gathered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other persons with you at that time? Who did you see on the street while you were going to this place called Skela?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: There were other men, women, and children there, and when we were on this field, there were some houses on fire next to the old slaughtering house, at the neighbourhood called Crnalici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Skela, did you proceed to any other place? Where did you proceed to?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: While we were there, the order came that the men should be separated from the women and children in that field. Afterwards the order came -- or rather some buses came to drive away the women and children. Then they stopped that and said that the older women and women and children could go back home. So only the men stayed behind, and then came buses and they loaded us onto those buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this stage did you recognise any person, or could you tell the Court who these people were who were giving orders and who were making the people get into buses?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: They were men under arms, soldiers in uniform. But the person giving orders over a loudspeaker was Zoran Babic, called Baki.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know this person before?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He used to train judo and karate in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he dressed, and was he armed at that stage?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: He was in uniform, olive-grey. He had an automatic rifle and a hand-held launcher as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This person by the name of Babic, do you know to which ethnic group he belonged?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified, saying that women, children, and men were put onto buses. Do you know to which ethnic group these people belonged?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: All those persons were of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that the men were put into buses. Could you tell the Court what happened thereafter, where the buses proceeded to?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: When I got onto a bus, my bus headed toward the centre of town; then it reached the Sipad company, turned at Jereza, to the right, and then to the left to SUP. When we reached the SUP building, the bus stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the people in the bus? Did you recognise any of the people in the bus that you travelled in?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: In the bus, we were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other persons other than the civilians?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: There were the security soldiers, Serb soldiers. There was one soldier who held a hand grenade in his hand, and as soon as we got into the bus he said, "Don't anyone try anything because if anyone does, I will throw this grenade."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that the bus came and stopped in front of the SUP building. How long did you all stay there, and what did the people do in the bus -- the people in the bus do?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: When the bus stopped, the guard got off and told us to get off. We started getting off and then someone else came and said, "Get off the back door, not the front door." We went back into the bus. Then a third man came and said, "Close the doors and drive them further."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from there, did you see where you all were taken to?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: The bus started. It turned next to the market. It was going towards the JNA building; then Partizanska; at Kanafa it turned left, towards Gomjenica and Cela.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were travelling in the bus, were you able to see outside?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: We were ordered to bend our heads but one could peep from under one's arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything outside while you were travelling?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: When we were turning left into Partizanska Street, in front of Kanafa, on the pavement there were three or four dead men lying there. And in Partizanska Street, houses on fire; they were Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that you saw on the street, you said "dead people," did you see whether they were civilians or whether they were people from the military or the forces?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: They were wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you saw some houses on fire. Did you recognise these houses? Were you able to identify these houses?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mustafa Cepic, the butcher Causevic, and Omer Ecimovic, who also had a cafe bar, so his house too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the buses stop thereafter, or were they stopped before their final destination?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: The bus was stopped once between Cela and Tomasica; there was a Serb checkpoint there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see as to what happened there or hear anything?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: They opened the door. The guard, he got off, and they were shouting from outside, "Let us have them so we can slaughter them, the motherfuckers."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who accompanied, or the guard who was in the bus, did he say anything, or did he allow the people to take any persons from the bus?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: No one got off. He got back into the bus, they closed the door, and we continued our journey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you finally arrive?

utterances.speaker: JASMIR OKIC
utterances.text: We finally arrived at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would stop at this stage and continue with the witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Waidyaratne. As we have said, I should like to communicate to the parties the agenda for tomorrow. We are having a Status Conference at 4.00. The first item will be judicial notice, you remember well that issue; a second item will be prior statements by witnesses, a question that has been raised by the parties, specifically by Mr. Fila; and a third item, the organisation of hearings. There's a whole series of things that we need to discuss and review. I should like to ask Madam Hollis whether you have any questions to add and which you would like us to address at the Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have one matter. It has come to our attention that it is possible that the accused Zigic will be raising an alibi defence, and if that is true, we would ask for the notice that is required under Rule 67 for alibi. So perhaps that can be covered tomorrow as well. I believe also, Your Honour, there is an outstanding objection to a photograph that the Prosecution tendered of a person with bruises on them, and I believe that needs to be addressed as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about the Defence? Do you have any questions for the Status Conference tomorrow so we can think about them in advance a little? Excuse me. Mr. Krstan Simic. I apologise, Mr. O'Sullivan. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] I speak in my own name, Your Honour. We will not have any particular questions except the question of prior statements of witnesses, the scope of those statements and the use of those statements. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan, are you speaking on behalf of the Defence team of Mr. Nikolic? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There is one outstanding issue, I believe. When we were last sitting, the issue came up of timeliness of objections under Rule 5 as relates to the formulation of questions by either the parties or by Your Honours. Briefly that question was raised. There were some submissions made. There may be other submissions for tomorrow and a ruling from Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan, this was already envisaged under the three items that I mentioned, that is, the court proceedings, but thank you for drawing our attention to that. Mr. Fila, no other questions? Mr. Tosic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have one question linked to the discussion we had with the Prosecution in connection with photographs of certain persons; in view of the fact that during the next few days we need to hear witnesses who did not recognise our defendant, our client, but by the description they gave in their statements, the allusions refer to quite different persons. And for those persons one could infer that our client was not the person, according to the statements of those mentioned witnesses. Those witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Tosic. We haven't started the Status Conference. I have indicated the items of the agenda, so I'm asking you to add to those items if you have anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the question is the photographs referred to by witnesses, and we will elaborate on our arguments during the Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Tosic. Mr. Jovan Simic, no? Nothing? You have nothing to add? Very well, then. We have all those items registered. The Status Conference will be at 4.00. We will be here at 9.30 to continue the hearing. Witness, we will see you again tomorrow morning. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
